Triggers.value: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly

Threat.value: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

Memory.value: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel like I don't know myself anymore
I can't deal with even the slightest upset
The event happened because of the way I acted

vignette:
Elena was twenty-four when she was taken. She had been a firefighter for two years, proud of her place on the crew, the first woman in her station’s history to make it past probation. The call came in for a warehouse fire on the south side—a four-alarm job that turned bad when a ceiling collapsed and she got separated from her team. She ended up pinned beneath a steel beam in a storage room, the door jammed shut by debris, the air thick with smoke and the sound of flames eating through the walls above her. It took nearly forty minutes for the rescue crew to cut through. She remembers the heat against her face, the way the light from the fire flickered through a crack in the door like a strobe, and the certainty that no one was coming. That certainty is what stays with her now, two years later, even though she was pulled out alive.

Elena lives alone in a small apartment near the station, but she has not been back to work in six months. The first sign of trouble came a few weeks after the fire, when she found herself flinching at the sound of the station’s alarm. She told herself it was normal, that anyone would be jumpy after what happened. But then the memories started arriving uninvited—not as stories she told herself, but as fragments that felt more real than her actual surroundings. She would be standing in the grocery store, reaching for a can of tomatoes, and suddenly she was back in that room, the heat pressing in, the crack of light pulsing. The memory felt like a photograph in her mind, vivid and sharp, but it also felt like it belonged to someone else—like she was watching a movie of a woman who was not her, pinned and helpless. That disconnect confused her more than the fear itself. She had always known who she was. Now she was not sure.

The triggers multiplied. Old photos of her crew, which she used to keep on her nightstand, now made her stomach turn; she boxed them up and slid them under her bed. Crowded spaces became unbearable. The firehouse common room, with its noise and bodies and overlapping voices, began to feel like a trap. She started eating lunch in her truck, then stopped coming in on her days off, then took a leave of absence. Each time she avoided a trigger, the relief was brief, but it confirmed something darker: that she could not handle even the smallest upset without feeling like she was falling apart. She blamed herself for the way she had acted during the fire—she had frozen, she thought, for a few seconds before the ceiling came down, and she was certain that hesitation was why she had been trapped. That self-blame became a loop. Every time she saw a photo or walked into a room with too many people, the thought returned: This is your fault. You are not the person you thought you were.

Elena’s sense of identity had dissolved. She no longer recognized the woman who had once run into burning buildings. That woman was competent, fearless, sure of her place. The woman she had become could not relax even in her own apartment, her body braced for a threat that never came. She startled at ordinary sounds—a car backfiring, a door slamming—and each time she jumped, the memory rushed back, sharp as a photograph. The memory itself made the world feel dangerous again, and the danger made the memory feel urgent, as if she needed to relive it to survive it. She began to monitor her environment constantly, scanning for exits, for signs of crowding, for anything that might trigger the next wave. But the scanning itself brought the triggers closer. She would notice a crowded aisle and think, I have to get out, and the thought would summon the memory of being trapped, and the memory would confirm that she was right to be afraid.

The cycle tightened over months. Elena stopped seeing friends because they wanted to meet in restaurants or bars, and she could not explain why a busy room made her feel like she was suffocating. She told herself she was weak. She told herself the fire had broken something in her that could not be fixed. The memories came more frequently now—not just in response to triggers, but on their own, unbidden, as if her mind had decided she needed to rehearse the worst moment of her life over and over. And each time the memory arrived, she felt the self-blame sharpen: You hesitated. You could have moved faster. You did this to yourself. The thought of returning to work felt impossible. The thought of never returning felt like a betrayal of everything she had been.

What finally brought Elena to therapy was a night in late October. She had been sitting on her couch, the apartment dark, when she heard a car door slam outside. She was on the floor before she knew she had moved, her heart pounding, the memory of the warehouse pressing in so vividly that she could smell the smoke. She stayed there for twenty minutes, unable to move, unable to tell herself she was safe. The next morning, she called a clinic. She is afraid of what she has become—afraid that the woman she used to be is gone for good—but she is also afraid that if she does not find a way out of this, she will spend the rest of her life waiting for a ceiling to fall.
